subtopic: REFERENCE TO UNEMPLOYMENT FIGURES FOR JANUARY, 1956

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REFERENCE TO UNEMPLOYMENT FIGURES FOR JANUARY, 1956
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. Has the minister any comment to make on the statistics which appeared in the papers this morning indicating that the unemployment figure for January is the second highest since the war?

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: REFERENCE TO UNEMPLOYMENT FIGURES FOR JANUARY, 1956
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the figures that appeared in the papers this morning were based upon the report which comes out from month to month. It gives a very complete survey of the situation as reflected over the period from the middle of December to the middle of January. I should like hon. members to recall that of course that is a period when there are a great number of lay-offs for one reason or another over the Christmas holidays and at the beginning of the year.
Up to that period our non-farm labour force in Canada had increased by 300,000, in round figures, since last year; and the total number of applicants for work were, in round figures, 100,000 less than last year. As a midwinter picture, while it is unfortunate there
are so many unemployed, I think we are in a better position this winter than we have been for a number of winters in the past regardless of the figures.
That is true in the main, of course, because of the buoyancy of our whole economy in Canada. To a much lesser degree it is true because of the fact that governments at all levels, industry-particularly the Canadian construction industry-labour unions, communities and municipalities have worked together on a very widespread experiment to see how seasonal unemployment might be attacked this winter. I hope and believe that we are learning many things that will be useful in the future. Finally, the improvement of the unemployment insurance plan, particularly during the seasonal period, is helping where more work cannot be obtained.

PARTICIPATION BY FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
At the adjournment last night I had been speaking for about a minute and a half on this amendment. At

the outset, I should like to say that I have not too much I want to put on the record. However, I feel we should review some of the things we have in mind in British Columbia in the field of power.
Of course atomic energy is something that is in the experimental stage at this time, and therefore there need not be too much said about it. On the other hand we know some advances have been made in the use of coal and gas for the production of electricity. In Alberta, for instance, the Calgary Light and Power Company is installing a plant at Wabamun that is going to develop about
147,000	horsepower. The information I have is that this plant is adapted to the use of gas but will eventually be converted to the use of coal. It is my understanding that the coal will be used in the form of dust in high pressure water tube boilers generating steam for turbines.
We can see that in this way electrical power is going to reach many people in Canada who otherwise would not have power because they are a long distance from hydroelectric plants. In that connection I should like to bring to the attention of the house a report appearing in the Dawson Creek Star of February 9, 1956. The heading is, "4200 Alberta farms get power in 1955." The article reads:
A total of 4,264 farms were organized into rural electrification associations during 1955, according to figures released today by the Hon. Raymond Reierson, minister of industries and labour. The number of farms electrified has now reached 34.768. In addition there are 5,410 non-farm customers who are receiving power as a result of the construction of farm lines.
There is no question but that the subject of power is important. The thing in which we are interested in Canada is how this power is going to reach the people of this country at the earliest possible moment and bring to them a higher standard of living. A good deal of our power in British Columbia is developed under a crown corporation known as the British Columbia Power Commission. In that province we fmd that under the power commission we have 150,000 kilowatts of hydroelectric power, 26,000 kilowatts of diesel, that is thermal electric, 700 miles of high voltage lines, and 3,300 miles of distribution lines.
I have been given to understand that there is a trend toward the use of direct current motors in industry, which give a great deal more power for the amount of electricity consumed. I also understand that experiments have been successful in the transmission of direct current over much longer distances than they are capable of transmitting alternating current at the present time. Because of these factors we can readily see that hydro 67509-88
Power Development
plants in some of the far reaches of our country can be brought, as it were, closer to the places where we have many farms and villages looking for electrical power.
It is expected that in British Columbia, owing to the gas line that is to be built from Fort St. John in the Peace river country to Vancouver, a great deal more thermal electric power will be developed through the use of gas. It is very important to realize that this great national resource is now to come to the people of British Columbia for power and heat. We are grateful for that. Many industries may develop in the interior of British Columbia as a result of the use of gas for both power and heat.
Possibly the position of British Columbia can best be summed up by referring to the federal-provincial co-operation in economic development submission made to this government on December 14, 1953. In the introductory remarks this is what the submission had to say:
The government of British Columbia in this brief proposes federal-provincial co-operation in the further economic development of the province and in the conservation of its natural resources. It submits that financial participation by the government of Canada in projects which will serve these purposes is warranted both by the national interest and by special consideration affecting British Columbia. It further submits that it is warranted by federal financial participation in projects in other parts of Canada. Accordingly, a joint program of public investment is here proposed.
I think that is in line with the amendment moved yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition.
The power potential of British Columbia is great. We have heard considerable mention of the Columbia river as a potential power site, but I should like to point out to the house that the Columbia river basin is by no means the largest and most important power site that we have in British Columbia. To mention a few, there is the Yukon Taku project. The potential there is almost 5 million horsepower as compared to the Columbia river development of 3,300,000 horsepower. The lower Fraser valley potential exceeds that of the Columbia river. The upper Fraser valley potential exceeds that of the Columbia river. These figures of the potential horsepower of British Columbia indicate that while a great deal of interest has been created in the Columbia river development project, a great deal of consideration has to be given to some of the other power sites in Canada.
We recognize, of course, that the fishing industry of British Columbia is an important factor and must receive its due consideration. In the known potential of British Columbia we have 22,913,000 horsepower and the

Power Development
potential of 25 per cent of the province is still unknown. That these developments will be of benefit not only to British Columbia but to the people of Canada is a fact I do not think anyone would care to deny.
The St. Lawrence seaway has been mentioned as being located in more or less the central part of Canada, and I believe that is true. I agree that a certain small amount of benefit may be derived in the over-all Canadian economy, and that is also true of such power projects as exist in British Columbia and in other parts of the country.
I would support the plea that the province of New Brunswick be given consideration in its Beechwood project. I think it is important to the economy of Canada that money is being spent in various parts of the nation for the development of power.
While I am on the subject of money I should like to say that it is certainly easy for hon. members of the opposition to be continually pressing the government for the expenditures of great sums of money, and it is perhaps not always possible for the government to meet our demands or requests. I believe I should use the word requests rather than demands; however, when I think back to about November 15 I recall that the Bank of Canada met with the chartered banks of this country. If I read the evidence correctly that meeting was for the purpose of recalling certain funds from specific areas with a view to making it more difficult to obtain credit in the country. In other words it was an indication that the money supply of the country was adequate to meet the demand for the distribution of goods.
If that is so, I would then say that the government had failed to meet its obligations some years ago when the decline in farm prices began. In this case where we are asking for federal money to be spent in various parts of Canada, the over-all money supply in the country must be taken into consideration because if the money supply is increased to the point where we are faced with inflation, we are then going to do more damage than ever to all the recipients of social assistance across the country whose living standard has been cut by the financial policies that have been followed by this government.
Speaking of money, which we know is necessary for the development of this country, I should like right now when the hon. gentleman over there says "real money" to quote an article which appeared in Labour of December 17, 1955, which is published in Washington. This reads:
How "Bankers' Money" Works
Uncle Sam's $205 billion national debt can keep on going up, but it can't come down much or
[Mr. Leboe.J
permanently without causing a depression. That's the surprising picture painted by economists at a Senate-House committee hearing on taxes.
The explanation, however, is this: The less money the government takes in taxes, the more it has to borrow from bankers. They "manufacture'' the money they lend to Uncle Sam when they buy his bonds. The government spends this "new money" and thus stimulates the economic machine.
What would happen if Uncle Sam used tax money to pay off part of the debt owed to bankers? The economists said that surely would cause an economic slump, for these reasons:
First, the people couldn't spend the money because it was taken from them in taxes. Second, the government couldn't spend money it used to pay off debt. Third, the debt payments would wipe out "bankers' money" circulating in the economic system.
It's a fine system for the bankers, because it yields them billions of dollars of profits in interest on the money they "manufacture". But is it the best possible system for the American people and their government?
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) suggested to the Social Crediters that we should support the use of the national credit. We do support 100 per cent the use of the national credit for the development of Canada, but we are not unmindful of the fact that the national debt of the United States has risen by billions -from $268 billion to approximately $300 billion. Many of those United States dollars have been reinvested in Canada as permanent capital, and that permanent capital investment in this country has added to the dollars released in the form of salaries, wages and dividends.
Once we have a sufficient money supply in the Dominion of Canada, surely we cannot ask the government to go into debt under the present financial policy, or that they should change it and use the Bank of Canada for the creation of money against the national credit to a point where we would have inflation. That is not a sound policy. Therefore I think we have to go back a good many years to find out exactly what caused the situation that we have today to develop. Having done so I think we will find that had we had a different financial policy in this country a good many years ago, many Canadians who today have not savings to invest would have savings to invest in this country.
Some suggestion was made that outside capital should not be invested in Canada for the development of our country. If that policy were to be followed it should have been followed many years ago. Take the Canadian Pacific Railway. I understand from the latest figure that 88 per cent of the dollar investment in the Canadian Pacific Railway comes from outside Canada. I understand the Aluminum Company of Canada is 75 per cent owned outside of Canada. In British Columbia, as mentioned before, we have the Kitimat project where a town of about 50,000 people

will eventually be built around that industrial development. That project was made possible by the investment of foreign capital together with Canadian capital.
All this business of what is socialism and what is free, responsible enterprise can be answered very quickly. Free, responsible enterprise is just exactly what it says and we can find out what socialism is in the Oxford Press dictionary, where it is very well explained. We do not need to be worrying about that here.
I was amazed to find that the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) did not rise on a question of privilege today and correct the speech he made yesterday with regard to the remarks he made concerning the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn). I suggest to the hon. member that he read in Hansard what the hon. member for New Westminster said and compare it with what he said he said. The same thing applies to the hon. member for Kootenay West. If he would do the same thing I am sure he would like to rise on a question of privilege and put the record straight.

In connection with power
development in Canada, I believe that in the past we have lost sight of the responsibility of governments to take the lead in encouraging the processing of our raw materials within our borders. I think there is much that can be done in all the provinces of Canada in that regard. Some of them are much worse off than others in that respect, and we know which ones they are. But surely we must get to the point where we are utilizing our own men and women in this country, who are looking for work, in the processing of our raw materials.
I can see no reason why, for instance, a pulp mill should be exporting pulp to another country. I do not see why we should not be making the paper right in this country instead of shipping the pulp out of the country. We should be shipping out newsprint, not pulp. In that respect I would advocate that due consideration should be

given by the government to rendering all the assistance necessary in the development of research, and that the government should encourage the full utilization and processing of our natural resources within our borders.
With respect to federal-provincial co-operation, I should like to refer to the proposal of the provincial government of British Columbia in their submission on December 14, 1953. I will not read the words, but on page 13 of their submission they pointed out that there were already certain precedents in Canada for dominion-provincial co-operation in those fields we have mentioned, and I would urge the government to take a new look at the situation.
If the money supply in Canada has reached the point where the release of further credit is going to cause inflation, then I think it is time the government made a full review of its financial policy and that of the Bank of Canada. I certainly can see no reason why we should not embark now on a policy that would bring about a situation whereby Canadians themselves would have the savings to invest in the development of their own country. Certainly we have not such a policy now, and that is what the hon. member for New Westminster pointed out yesterday. With reference to the provinces of western Canada he said, as found at page 1354 of Hansard:
They are prepared to accept United States investment, British investment, or investment from any other country that we can interest to the extent of coming into this country, provided they come in under our regulations.
In order to call what he said to the attention particularly of the hon. member for Vancouver South and the hon. member for Kootenay West, may I point out that he used these words, "provided they come in under our regulations." Naturally these provinces are looking to the protection of the interests of their people, and to seeing that their rightful share comes back to them from the processing of their natural resources. Therefore I think there is room for federal participation in the development of power if and when the time arrives that the federal government is in a position to do so.

subtopic: PARTICIPATION BY FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity of rising this afternoon to support quite briefly the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition yesterday. The pertinent part of that amendment reads as follows:
. . . consideration should be given to a joint investment program for the development of power resources in any province where the government of such province requests the co-operation of the Canadian government in carrying out such development.

Power Development
The Leader of the Opposition dealt with the problem on the broad national basis and left it to the rest of us to apply the broad principles to our particular provinces. I should like to emphasize two words in the amendment, the one "joint" and the other "co-operation". Joint investment certainly presupposes that there should be intimate and close co-operation.
I think the amendment is very timely, because only last year we had the sorry spectacle of two governments, the government of British Columbia and the federal government, failing lamentably to show the degree of co-operation that is necessary and will be necessary in the future if these joint programs are to work to the benefit of the people of any particular province or, in fact, to the benefit of the people of Canada as a whole. Of course I refer to that striking lack of co-operation which was shown in the early stages during the events that led up to the introduction of the international rivers bill.
I am not going to repeat today the details of that lack of co-operation. They are well known to all members of this house and to the majority of the people resident in British Columbia. It was indeed a sorry spectacle. However, after the bill had been amended we of this party were in support of the act as it was subsequently modified.
It will be recalled that under that act the federal government has the authority to issue a licence for the construction of any project on an international river. If the federal government assumed the authority to issue licences, it must also accept the responsibility which goes with that authority which it has taken. If the federal government merely adopts a negative attitude and says it will not issue licences for this or that project which may be suggested either by the provincial government or by some corporation anxious to develop the industrial resources of any particular international river, there will be a great deal of resentment. In fact, the people will never tolerate such an attitude.
Industry today is straining every nerve to find additional sources of power. The assumption of this authority by the federal government is a challenge to the government which it must accept, namely the challenge to assist Canadians to retain and develop the power resources of Canada in the best interests of the Canadian people. We are today faced with organizations, corporations, businessmen and industrialists in the United States who are only too anxious to come in, build projects on
IMr. Pearkes.l
our rivers and utilize the power which is produced from those projects for the power-hungry industries of the United States, giving to Canada or, in the case of British Columbia, to the province of British Columbia only a portion of the wealth in power which they have taken from our own waters. I therefore feel that it is a definite challenge to this federal government to see that it adopts a positive attitude toward the development of these streams.
Until quite recently coal was the main source of power in British Columbia. However, that day has gone. In British Columbia our coal fields, I regret to say, are not as active as they were. Many of the seams have played out. Today water is providing 44 per cent of the power, petroleum provides 38 per cent and coal has dropped in position until it is providing only 18 per cent. The estimates which have been made indicate that there will be a considerable increase in the proportion of power provided by water. In fact some scientists have estimated that not less than 70 per cent of our power will be derived from water sources in the near future.
The hydroelectric potential in British Columbia, based upon careful surveys carried out by the water comptroller of that province, has been estimated as something over 25 million horsepower. But today in the installed hydro stations we are producing only 2,246,000 horsepower. Those figures show what a tremendous increase there may be, from 2 million horsepower to 25 million horsepower, for all of which sources have been located. There are still large portions of the province, particularly in the northeastern part of British Columbia, where no surveys have yet been made. The availability of the horsepower which has so far been developed has played a major part in the development of our mining and smelting industry. It is therefore quite obvious that if we can develop that enormous potential to 25 million horsepower or more, the growth of British Columbia in population and in industry will be beyond imagination.
Just to give some idea of the various localities where there has been development-and there are still projects which are undeveloped but which have been surveyed-I start out by giving the figures around Vancouver island, which are contrary to the general trend in the rest of the province. On Vancouver island there are 396,000 horsepower developed but undeveloped there remain only 235,000 horsepower. Obviously there is an acute shortage in sight on Vancouver

island. It is for that reason that this year a cable is being laid to bring power from the mainland of British Columbia to Vancouver island.
When we come onto the mainland, in the lower Fraser valley we And that only
986.000	horsepower have been developed. That is in the immediate vicinity of the metropolitan area of Vancouver. Yet the surveys have shown that 3,600,000 horsepower are available. Up the Columbia river only 703,000 horsepower have been developed, while again there are 3,300,000 horsepower which are undeveloped. In what is termed the upper Fraser district there are no developments; no projects have been developed. Yet according to the surveys which have already been made, 3,600,000 horsepower are available. In the Kitimat area only the small quantity of 560,000 horsepower have been developed while the undeveloped sources reach the figure of 2,240,000 horsepower.
Then as we go further north into that immense area of the Yukon Taku district, there are no water power developments there but the estimated undeveloped potential is
4.900.000	horsepower. As I said a moment ago, the northeastern portion of the province has not even been surveyed.
I think those figures give some idea of the future prospects of this great province. The hydroelectric developments which have taken place so far have been of the nature of single and steep developments on individual sites. It is probable that in future developments, particularly the type of development that is expected in the lower Fraser valley, the trend which has been taking place in the United States will be followed. This means the multiple use of the water, so that wherever it is economical to put in irrigation plants as well as power plants, the two will be developed concurrently.
With these great possibilities ahead I must sound a note of caution, or perhaps it may be even a further challenge to the government. No dam or hydro project must be developed on our streams on the west coast without due consideration being given to the effect upon our fisheries. Of course the principal fishery in British Columbia is salmon. The estimated market value of that fishery in a normal year, such as last year, is over 50 million. This industry employs, as fishermen and in allied occupations, well over
15.000	people.
The problem of passing fish over a dam in a river is as old as dam construction itself, but until comparatively recent years dams in most rivers were very low and the engineers and fishermen who gave any
Power Development
consideration to this problem were concerned with the upward movement of the fish. A few ladders enabled the fish to work their way up to the spawning grounds. But as dams were built higher and higher it became noticeable that in spite of the fish ladders which were provided the run of fish in those particular streams was decreasing.
Perhaps I might digress for a moment to give a very brief life history of our Pacific salmon. It is common knowledge that during the summer and fall months the salmon work up from the ocean to the spawning grounds in fresh water, literally hundreds of miles from the seashore. There the salmon spawn and immediately die. During the winter months the eggs lie dormant, but they are hatched early in the spring. By April the small fry are free swimming. Some species, such as the pinks, work their way down to the ocean immediately so you have the problem of little fry, two inches in length, going down and encountering a dam and wondering how to get past that obstruction.
Other types of fish, such as the sockeye and spring, remain in the fresh water for one, two or three years, and reach a length of six to eight inches before they start to work down the streams. If they meet a dam they have to find a way to get around it or over it. The problem presented to the engineers is entirely different according to the species with which they are dealing. Following their natural instincts the fry or fingerlings follow the main stream, and if there is water spilling over the dam they follow that spillway and are hurled hundreds of feet to the lower level. Obviously the casualties from abrasion and from the sudden change in height and pressure is very high. If there is no water running over the top of the dam, no surface spillway, then the fish are either shut in or they must go through some submerged spillway or through the turbines. In both cases the results of course is a very heavy death toll.
It was only when the higher dams were being built that the engineers realized that the greatest damage to the fishing industry was done when the fish were migrating downstream rather than upstream. A few years ago a series of investigations were carried out by Canadian and United States officials under the international pacific salmon fisheries commission at Baker dam in north Washington. The Baker dam is only a comparatively high dam, 250 feet. Dams now built or being built are two to three times that height. As a result of the investigations which were carried out it was found that 64 per cent of the sockeye which went over the spillway were killed, and 34 per cent of the sockeye

Power Development
which went through the turbines were killed. This gives some idea of the problem and indicates that unless this problem of passing fish over, through or under these projects is tackled there will soon be no fishing industry on the west coast, or else the power developments will be limited to the non-fish streams. Neither of these results would be desirable.
If our hydro development is limited to the non-fish stream, then a great deal of that enormous potential to which I referred may not be realized. We cannot, of course, contemplate having hydro plants built on fish-producing streams that otherwise would ruin the fishing industry until some way has been found by which the fish may be passed safely around, through or under these dams. I am pleased to say that experiments are being carried out now which are meeting with a degree of success. I have myself seen fish led around in a tank by electrical methods. It is quite easy to do that in an experimental tank, but there are great difficulties when it comes to the question of guiding millions of small fish in an open stream. However, the project is being examined.
Experiments are being carried out, but I regret to say that the majority of those experiments are being carried out in the United States by the United States corps of engineers. They are spending annually something like $400,000 in just carrying out these experiments. A small grant has been made to the University of British Columbia, and I believe something in the neighbourhood of $60,000 is to be spent this year in my province.
I say that these are the two challenges to this government. If they sit down and do nothing about the development of our rivers, and if they will not examine into and produce some results regarding fish migration so that the streams and rivers of British Columbia can be used both for hydro development and for fish production, then they will have fallen short of the task which they should undertake.
These great projects cannot be undertaken by one government alone. As this amendment points out, these must be joint investments with the co-operation of the provincial governments. Therefore I do urge this government to tackle this job seriously and to enter into the fullest and closest co-operation with the provincial governments in order that Canadians may get the full benefit of their resources and we shall not see them being developed and taken away from us by the United States, or by any foreign concern.

subtopic: PARTICIPATION BY FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this afternoon, again at the

risk of being styled an expert in the field of engineering by some of the western members. However, I should like to say a word on power as it affects the province of New Brunswick. We do not need hon. members from the west down in New Brunswick to teach us Social Credit doctrine, either.

subtopic: PARTICIPATION BY FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL AUTHORITIES
speechtext: Why did you invite us?

subtopic: PARTICIPATION BY FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
You invited yourselves. When I came to this house I had the honour and privilege of being associated with and having for my office mate Mr. J. G. Boucher, who was for a number of years the chairman of the electric power commission, or the hydro commission, whatever the proper title is, in the province of New Brunswick. Mr. Boucher, while in office in New Brunswick, laid out a policy of thermol units that I believe will be followed some time in the future by the present authorities.
I shall leave the Beech wood project to some of my colleagues from New Brunswick to go into fully. I will say in passing, however, that in the Moncton Transcript of February 18,	1956, Mr. Cleophas Leger,
M.L.A., says this about Beechwood:
Turning to Beechwood, Mr. Leger contended the province could build the project on its own resources, claiming tax rental funds would be sufficient "if this government did not waste it elsewhere."
That is the government of New Brunswick.
He charged that the Flemming administration "had in its hands a good part of the money needed for Beechwood and it came from Ottawa. But the government frittered it away on less important things".
He said first things were not given first consideration. He added that federal help to the province had been steady in the past and more would be available when "we are prepared to use it wisely, without wasting it".
I should now like to compare the potential industrial expansion of the province of New Brunswick with the New England states. During the course of my remarks I shall be using figures that come from a survey called "Power in New England", a report of the power survey committee of New England council, the chairman of which was E. H. Hunter, chairman, New Hampshire public service commission; from Maine, Edward E. Chase, president, Maine Securities Company, Portland; Bryant L. Hopkins, engineer, Kennebec Water Power Company, Waterville. Associated with these men were approximately 20 or 25 men from the states of New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts', Rhode Island and Connecticut.
In their report they publish a bibliography which has the following authorities: Published reports of federal power commission; published reports of Edison electric institute; published reports of corps of engineers, U.S.

army; statistical abstracts, United States department of commerce; water supply papers, United States geological survey; congressional reports on St. Lawrence seaway project's; journal of Boston society of civil engineers; publications of national electric light association; reports to public service commission of Vermont on flood control power and storage projects by H. K. Barrows; report to associated industries of Massachusetts of its power investigating committee, 1924; reports of Maine state water power commission; reports of New Hampshire water resources board; reports of Maine public utilities water power and storage commission; report on development of inland waterways of Massachusetts by special commission; water resources of New England, New England regional planning commission; report of the special commission on regional planning commission; report of the special commission on the development of inland waterways, 1947, commonwealth of Massachusetts.
I wanted to have my authorities on the record so the report could not be considered as a trivial one. Because water power was a prime factor in the original development of industrial communities in New England it has become magnified in the minds of many with respect to the present situation. Hydroelectric power is cheap only in the most favourable locations, of which few remain undeveloped; and of all the industries of New England using water power, perhaps the only one in which the cost of power might be a determinant factor in its location is the pulp and paper industry.
During the depression years between 1929 and 1939 a number of industrial-owned power plants were discontinued, and the output fell from 1,800,000 kilowatts to 1,200,000 kilowatts. During the war years this reduction in the production of power ceased and it increased somewhat. Since V-J day 1,144,000 kilowatts of capacity either have been constructed, were under construction or are on order in New England. All this capacity will be in use by 1951; this is the report of 1948.
Ninety-one per cent of this new capacity is owned by utilities, and of the new capacity 91 per cent is steam power. This capacity will build up reserves that were depleted during the war years; and 81 per cent of the new capacity will be located in Massachusetts, Connecticut and Rhode Island. From 65 to 75 per cent of all electrical energy generated in New England in the 1948 period came from steam plants. In the United States as a whole from 60 to 65 per cent of the energy generated is from steam plants. The exact percentage from year to year depends
Power Development
upon the rainfall and the extent to which the hydro development plants can be operated.
This predominance of steam generated power will be accentuated in the future because the number of feasible undeveloped water power sources is limited. It is therefore logical that the cost of steam power is the best comparison for determining the economic feasibility of hydro developments. During the last century steam generating plants have increased in size, efficiency and complexity. They are now built in locations where coal and oil are available, and where water for condensation is readily accessible.
I should like to put on record a table with respect to New England. In Massachusetts electricity produced by utilities was 1,254,000 kilowatts; 592,000 kilowatts was produced by industrial corporations, the total being
1.846.000	kilowatts of which 87-8 per cent was generated by steam power.
In Rhode Island utilities produced 319,000 kilowatts; industry produced 78,000 kilowatts, a total of 397,000 kilowatts of which 96 per cent was produced by steam generated plants.
In Connecticut 828,000 kilowatts were produced by utilities; 246,000 kilowatts was produced by industrial producers, a total of
1.074.000	kilowatts. Of this power 90-3 per cent was produced by steam generating plants.
In New England as a whole 2,617,000 kilowatts was produced by utilities and 1,079,000 was produced by industrial corporations, a total of 3,696,000 kilowatts. The over-all percentage for New England power produced by steam generated plants was 74 per cent.
The annual cost of power available from steam plants is made up of two components, the first of which is capacity cost. This is composed of annual fixed charges on the capital investment plus the annual operating and maintenance expense. The second is energy cost, which is the fuel cost expressed in mills per kilowatt hour. The coal which is used in New England averages about 13,500 B.t.u. per pound as received. On this basis the 1947 cost of coal in Boston was about $7-80 per ton.
It appears to me that in the province of New Brunswick, with its limited water power sites that are feasible for harnessing, and perhaps more so in the province of Nova Scotia, we must turn to the thermo method of generating electricity. I believe the normal increase in the use of electricity will take up any hydroelectric power that is generated in the next several years in the province of New Brunswick. As has been pointed out in this

Power Development
report, the use to which hydroelectric plants can be fully put depends upon the rainfall. For example, last year in New Brunswick we had a very dry summer. Last year would be a model year for the combining of thermo power and hydroelectric power. In the province of New Brunswick we have the coal fields at Minto, and in addition to that we have vast coal reserves in our neighbouring province of Nova Scotia.
This committee reached some conclusions in their report, and I should like to read a paragraph or two of those conclusions, as follows:
New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut use about 89 per cent of the utility power produced in New England and constitute an integrated system. This area is dependent on steam power for the major part of its power needs because at present about 80 per cent of the generating capacity is steam. Even if all the undeveloped hydro power in this area were built regardless of whether it is economically feasible or not, it would not take care of half the expected increase in load during the next ten years. Therefore it is obvious that a large addition to the steam capacity will be required.
The report has this to say concerning the cost of power in manufacturing:
The importance of the cost of power in manufacturing has been greatly overemphasized. Except in a few industries the cost of power averages less than 2 per cent of the total value of manufactured products in New England industries. It is, therefore, obvious that the question of cheap power is not a determining factor in management decisions regarding location of manufacturing plants except for certain heavy industries. Other factors such as labour, markets, and materials are the principal ones which govern these decisions. A change in power rates which affects such a small part of the value of a product has an extremely minor effect on its total cost, but the importance of having a source available which provides reliable power when it is required cannot be overemphasized.
I believe that in the province of New Brunswick and in the Maritime provinces as a whole we are somewhat in the same situation as the New England states. No one can deny that the New England states, especially the area centred around the state of Massachusetts, are highly industrialized. They have no greater hydroelectric potential in those states than we have in the maritime provinces, but of course they do have a geographic advantage with respect to markets.
I believe that the policies laid down by the late J. G. Boucher of New Brunswick hydro power commission should be dusted off in many offices in New Brunswick, and then I feel that within a short time the province of New Brunswick will come back to a combined system of thermal and hydroelectric power.

Following this report the Electrical World of November 27, 1948, had this to say about it:
New England Must Rely on Fuel,
Not Hydro Power
Fuel-generated electricity must be the backbone of New England's power supply for many years to come. Valuable as economically warranted hydro may be, there simply is not enough of it undeveloped and practicable in the northeast to meet New England's needed 1,100,000-kw generating-plant expansion in the next decade.
And later:
The report points out that the importance of the cost of power in manufacturing has been greatly overemphasized. In textiles, power is but 2-3 per cent of the total cost. For industry as a whole in the area, it is but H per cent.
I realize that the conditions in New England are not on all fours with those in New Brunswick, but I believe the ideas and findings contained in the report of that committee would be of assistance to New Brunswick. As I said previously, I wished only to place the importance of the generation of electricity by coal before this house. My colleagues from New Brunswick will deal with the development of hydroelectric power, but hydroelectric power alone is not enough for the province of New Brunswick; we must have thermo-developed power as well.

subtopic: PARTICIPATION BY FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been some very interesting comments made during the course of this debate. In fact the very first speech contained some extremely interesting comments including an invitation to political merger- I said merger, not murder.
I should like to deal with that for a moment. I was most interested in the invitation of the Leader of the Opposition that the two parties sitting in this corner of the house should combine with the Conservative party. It is with the utmost regret and respect that on behalf of this group I must decline the proposal. I do not think I can even give the traditional answer of the coy maiden and say that we shall be a sister to them.
On the other hand there is a field in which I think we could do a little cultivation with some benefit. I would suggest to the hon. gentleman that he follow the example of his former party colleague, the premier of British Columbia, who having discovered that the old gray mare of Conservatism was not what she used to be in British Columbia, very nimbly leaped from her on to the back of the piebald pony, Social Credit, and rode into power.
In case the Leader of the Opposition thinks there is any danger in this manoeuvre I would commend that he follow even more closely

the activities of the premier of British Columbia, for he will find that the Social Credit party is still quite firmly in the grip of two gentlemen, who not so very long ago were members of the Progressive Conservative party. I am not sure that the Leader of the Opposition is as politically agile as is the premier of British Columbia, but I believe the premier of British Columbia would be prepared to give him a course of lessons at a reasonable rate of remuneration.
I am convinced that this is the wisest policy for the Conservative party, even more so after having listened to the speech of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) yesterday. Just in case I might be accused of misquoting him, I should like to place some of his words back on Hansard. They will be well worn words by the time Hansard gets through with them. I quote from page 1352 of Hansard of February 20, where the hon. member is reported as follows:
It might be said, why cannot the people of Canada finance that development? I am satisfied that you realize as well as I do, as do most of our socialist-minded friends, that you cannot build a huge dam for nothing; that is just wishful thinking. Some of these dams cost anywhere from $300 million to $750 million. It takes a great deal more capital than the Canadian public can afford to invest within the country for its proper development. We lack the capital for proper development.
Dear, dear, Mr. Speaker; this is from the party which has been enunciating with monotonous regularity, rather like an incantation, throughout the country that what is physically possible is financially possible. It removes the last possible obstacle to fusion between the two parties to the right in Canada. I am quite sure that the rest of us will be only too delighted to come to dance at the wedding.
Nevertheless I welcome this curious, shall I say rather un-Conservative, proposal that has been brought before the house. But like Oliver Twist I ask for more. I do not think it goes quite far enough. It is a very good thing to suggest that the people of Canada through the federal and provincial governments should co-operate in the development and production of power, but I think we have to ask ourselves something else. We have to ask ourselves for what purpose are we producing this power?
Mention has been made in the house of the Kitimat development in British Columbia. As has been quite rightly said, it is a most stupendous engineering project. However, it was accompanied by some rather dismaying results that were not envisaged because there was no over-all planning of that particular scheme. I refer of course to the devastation that occurred in Tweedsmuir park, much of 67509-89
Power Development
which could have been avoided had there been a long-term plan prepared well in advance for the logging of that area. That project has earned a rather unenviable reputation with regard to certain aspects of the conditions under which the workers in that area must work.
For a number of years we have had in British Columbia a publicly-owned power commission. I was in the provincial legislature when the power commission was set up. That commission has been engaged in very important development work, particularly on Vancouver island. However, it has been suffering from some severe handicaps imposed upon it by various governments in British Columbia. I think it is true enough to say that it was gone ahead with and developed for one purpose and one purpose only, to provide cheap power for certain large industries which were about to be established on Vancouver island.
Its devotion of power to those purposes makes me think that we should ask some further questions. For instance, we should ask this question. Is it enough to plan to produce power to supply a pulp and paper mill which as parts of its operations is going to produce raw material for the comics which the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) has been fighting so vigorously for a number of years, simply to add to the flow of trash which comes from the printing presses? Are we to be satisfied with merely providing power and letting those who receive it go on and use it as they will.
No, Mr. Speaker; we have had a lot of warnings lately, and these warnings have come from people to whom I think we should listen very carefully. Quite prominent among the voices have been those of Canada's Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair). They have been bringing us some very serious news about which we should be thinking very carefully.
The main warnings they have been bringing us are these. They warn us that it is only at our peril that we underestimate the industrial and economic capacities of the communist world. They warn us also that we shall be running very severe risks if we harbour the comforting illusion that the peoples of the communist world are in a state of incipient revolt, for the evidence they have brought us indicates that the exact contrary is the case and that the people in that area are not only supporting their government but apparently supporting it with considerable enthusiasm in the pursuit of a certain goal.
I should say at this point, Mr. Speaker, that no Liberal, no Conservative, no supporter of

Power Development
private enterprise can have experienced one-quarter of the dismay and the disillusion experienced by socialists regarding some of the developments within the Soviet union over the last 30 years. Only a socialist, I suppose, could have had that disillusionment at seeing what began and what might have continued as a noble experiment in human relations and social organization degenerate through the years and develop many aspects of squalid tragedy and repression of human dignity.
Nevertheless, as this rising chorus of warning voices tells us, merely because we have been disillusioned with what has gone on there, merely because we see with all too clear eyes the tremendous gap there is between the socialist ultimate aim and what has been accomplished in the communist world, we would do well not to delude ourselves into thinking that because we do not like some of its aspects'it is not an economically viable and valid regime; a regime, moreover, that is at the present moment offering the greatest threat to people of our type of thinking in the world. It is offering a threat because it has developed that enormous industrial potential, and the reason it has developed that enormous industrial potential in the short space of one generation is perfectly plain and perfectly simple for anyone to read. There has been deliberate, conscious planning of the development of resources and power in that country for a specific purpose.
We may have our doubts about what the ultimate purposes of that planning are, and no one knows; but one of its by-products is that it has developed an industrial machine there that those in this country who should know warn us threatens our supremacy in North America in the industrial world. I think when we are considering the question of developing our power we should be considering that thought, as to what is the purpose of our production in this country. I have been amused sometimes at the comfort that certain people in Canada and the United States have taken from the plainly much lower living standards of the peoples in the communist world. They have deluded themselves into thinking that these lower standards are a sign of the incompetence of the Soviet economic machine, and of course all they are a sign of is the ruthless efficiency of a totalitarian regime that can make economic plans without too much consideration for the happiness or convenience or comfort of the members of its society.

subtopic: PARTICIPATION BY FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL AUTHORITIES
speechtext: You would not advocate that, would you?

subtopic: PARTICIPATION BY FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
I am not advocating it, but I am suggesting it would be even more foolish to pretend that it does not exist and that it is not an effective method of producing goods of certain qualities, certain varieties and estimated in determined quantities. I also suggest that here in North America we run very serious risks if we think we are going to be able to compete with that sort of danger by the haphazard, unplanned type of production in which we engage today. It is not good enough merely to plan where we are going to get a source of power to operate our industries. We have to plan also as we planned during the last war. We have to plan to do it without unnecessary waste of our resources.
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, just how long the people of North America are going to go on smugly deluding themselves that they can continue to destroy natural resources like a horde of hungry locusts for the most trivial and childish aims. How much longer are we going to make the goal of our industrial and social life bigger and better automobiles to cause more problems in our cities? How much longer are we going to continue to haggle over the appropriation of a few million dollars to improve our admittedly inadequate educational system, while at the same time we observe with complacency the investment of millions upon millions of dollars in the production of useless trash for the debilitation of our population?
Has anybody thought to compare the cost of establishing, shall we say, one of these junior colleges that the province of Ontario has announced it is about to establish with the cost of producing astronomical numbers of bottles of pop to rot our children's teeth? That is the sort of thing we are doing with our resources today, and I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot very much longer go on doing that sort of thing without heading straight for disaster.
We could do it when North America stood without a peer in the world for industrial capacity and efficiency, but it is doubtful now that we stand in that position. We persist of course in continuing a standard of living, that standard which Thorstein Veblen has called conspicuous waste, and we have developed an elaborate advertising racket to pander to the very lowest, cheapest and silliest desires of our people in order to create a market for the production of trash in great quantities.
I have wondered just how long we are going to blind ourselves to this very difficult position that we are in today, and when we are going to realize that we have a supremely difficult task to perform. It is true enough

that in North America and in Canada we have in our society values which are supremely well worth preserving, values and standards that are perhaps the fine flower of human thinking, alongside this invitation to low standards that goes on under the pressure of modern business. We have to solve the problem of meeting our communist opponents on the field of industrial production while at the same time preserving for ourselves those elements of our society without which we would find life intolerable, and it is not going to be an easy job to do.
But, Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in saying that sooner or later our production is going to be planned by someone. Either we are going to undertake it ourselves on a rational basis; either we are going to set ourselves goals as we set them during the war, or someone else is going to do that planning and is going to do it with ruthlessness, in the same way it is being done in other parts of the world. We cannot escape that problem today.
The whole world is moving now toward the field of rational economic planning, and the Conservative amendment that has been produced here is a sign of that trend today. I am not in any way jeering at my Conservative friends when I suggest that only a few years ago their predecessors would have hesitated for a long time before they would have come into the house and advocated public investment. It is a step toward that goal of rational economic planning which we must meet if we are to survive in the world today. While it is true enough that we do not like what we see going on on the other side of the world, and while it is true enough that individual liberties have been trampled on, I sometimes wonder whether we do not embrace too large a territory under the spreading umbrella of liberty and freedom in this part of the world.
Is it really essential, Mr. Speaker, for the preservation of human liberties that individuals and groups of individuals should be left free to decide what they are going to do with our natural resources, at what rate they will consume them and what commodities they will make from them, without any regard whatever to the public welfare and without any regard whatever to a concerted, integrated social aim? That is the question we must answer and, in my opinion, we must answer it quickly. I suspect that sitting in this house are members who will, before many years, sit here and hear proposals which today would be denounced as rank bolshevism, and they will probably come from the most respectable quarters of this house when, 67509-89J
Power Development
under the heat of economic reality, fear, prejudice and superstition have been dissolved.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I welcome the amendment of our Conservative friends. I wish it went further. For my part I expect to see before long not only resolutions in this house but actual undertakings in Canada along the lines of those of which I have spoken. I believe that not even the most purblind of our people will want to run the risk of extinction merely in order to uphold the shibboleth of liberty of man to exploit his fellow man, which is what we lump in under the whole general concept of freedom and liberty today. I believe that our people eventually, and before long, will awake to the fact that their individual liberty and freedom can be found only in a rational society in which the resources-including electric power resources and the other natural and human resources-are devoted to a certain determined and approved social goal.

subtopic: PARTICIPATION BY FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to be able to take a short time this afternoon to speak in support of this resolution. It illustrates a line of thinking which is not particularly new to me. I think we should keep in mind what the resolution indicates. There is a tendency to get off on one branch of it and to concentrate too much on one phase of power. That is what rather surprised me about my colleague from New Brunswick, the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy) when he was speaking this afternoon. I felt that he was against this suggestion. Maybe that is not so. I could not help wondering whether he is against hydroelectric development. I think this resolution covers the field of power from any source whatsoever. It is a co-operative affair.
We all realize that the development of power is within the jurisdiction of the provinces, and there is no indication, as a result of the suggestion in this resolution, that the situation should be otherwise. But it seems to me that in this federation of ours we are a family of provinces. We have our interprovincial boundaries. We have a long boundary between Canada and the United States of America. Hence we have our international problems.
These problems arise in many ways immediately you commence to consider the development of our resources. As soon as you start to consider industry, one of the first things about which they talk is the matter of power. Regardless of what may have been said here today, the cheaper the power the more inducement there is to industry. It is true that other things must be taken into

Power Development
consideration. The fact that we have interprovincial and international problems in this country seems to me to constitute a reason why there should be evolved a national policy whereby, in all these situations, there should be co-operation between the dominion and the provincial authorities.
There may be many situations in which a province does not want the co-operation of the federal government. In such a situation I do not think the federal authority should impose its will upon the province. But I believe there are many situations in which co-operation is required. As was mentioned previously, it is more or less left to members from various provinces to deal with specific areas.
I have reference to the situation in which we find ourselves in my province. We have interprovincial problems and international problems there. We have possibilities of development which involve the crossing of not only provincial but international boundaries. I am not going to spend any time in going into all the details of this matter, because I know the government have those details. Surveys, investigations and recommendations have been made. The point, however, is this. If any province has a sound policy of resources development-and I contend that we in my province come within the bounds of what I am going to say-and if there is a demand for the product of those resources but unfortunately owing to size there is lack of financial backing, it should have a right and should expect to go to the central authority that sits over all the provinces and put forward its proposition. I think it has a right to expect that the central or federal authority will give serious and sympathetic consideration to the development of the type of policy which a province outlines if it comes within those suggestions I have made. There may be others. I refer to a development that is found to be possible and where there is a market for the product.
I contend that we in New Brunswick are practically in that position. For years after confederation our industrial activity declined. If I had the time in which to do so, there are many things I should like to say about that matter. The hon. member for Westmorland when speaking a few days ago-I do not know how many figures he put on the record -gave this house a picture of what happened and gave a picture of how our industrial activity declined.
At the time of confederation or shortly thereafter, of the four provinces that went into confederation, my province had the highest percentage of population employed in industry. It had quite a margin, as a matter of fact. The figure was 6-3 per cent, and the

average in Quebec and Ontario was only 5 * 50 per cent. In the years that have elapsed since then we have gone down to less than 4 per cent. Today we stand second to the lowest, while those other provinces have gone up to more than double.
It does seem to me that the intent of the planners of confederation was that generally speaking, possibly with some minor exceptions here and there, all parts of this country should develop at an even pace. It seems to me the idea was that the federal authority was to act as a levelling force where necessary to help each and every area in order that one area might not become dependent upon another. Within the last few years that is the position in which we have found ourselves. We hear it said that maritimers are always coming with our hands out. Being a maritimer I do not like to hear that, but we cannot say too much about it. I have heard it since I have come to Ottawa. We would like to be in a position in my province where we do not have to do that.
Within the last few years there have been tremendous mineral discoveries in New Brunswick, and with the development of those mineral resources it would appear that we could become not only self-supporting but contributors to the rest of this country. We have a fairly bright future. The one block in our way at the moment is power. The reason I like this resolution is this. We in New Brunswick-I should like to tell this to the hon. member for Westmorland but I think he must know it-are developing thermal power right along with our hydro power. We are not concentrating on hydro at all. There are not sufficient potential hydro sites available that have been surveyed and approved at the moment to meet the demands we know we must meet within the next 10 years. We cannot, therefore, hold up this program in which the federal authority may join with the provincial authority. If the federal and provincial authorities in cooperation feel that they can develop thermal power to better advantage, that is all right. We have no objection to that. What we need is power.
Last evening the hon. member for Inver-ness-Richmond (Mr. MacEachen) referred to the report of the Atlantic provinces economic council. I agree with those who spoke on this subject. I think this is the beginning of an organization which is going to be of great advantage to the Atlantic region. The hon. member referred to certain statements in that report which apply to the region as a whole. I should like to refer, Mr. Speaker, to some of the specific findings in that report which refer to my province of New Brunswick. Last September the council held what

was called an economic seminar at the University of New Brunswick. Apparently it was attended by some of the outstanding men in Canada and the New England states. I will not quote too much, but I should like to quote a few lines showing who these people were. The report says:
In September, 1955, at the University of New Brunswick in Fredericton, we held an economic seminar which, to say the least produced encouraging results. Information and background on a wide range of economic problems facing the Atlantic region were discussed. An exchange of ideas between leading men in economic, government, business and professional fields were possible. Excellent representation by well informed personnel from the federal government, provincial governments, the universities, the New England council, research associations and business entities participated whole heartedly to make this seminar an outstanding success.
I am not going to read too much of the report, but further down it says:
The seminar discussed at some length the opportunity for secondary manufacturing industries to develop in the region. That is, to provide profitable employment for the people displaced in the development of the primary industries.
Anyone who is interested may read the whole of the report, but I do not want to take that time. However, it says:
In New Brunswick, for example, if large quantities of relatively cheap power are made available, primary mineralogical extraction could be supplemented by processing at points of power generation and large chemical industries established. Before getting into my short talk on power, I should like to refer briefly to the humorous remarks of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) about horseback riders, weddings and so on that have been taking place in British Columbia. I should like to tell the hon. member and all hon. members that we in the Social Credit party do not enlarge our group by marriage but rather by adoption. I would invite all forwardthinking Canadians to renounce the Conservative, Liberal and socialistic theories they may have had and join our happy family.

I come now to the amendment which we support wholeheartedly. However, there is one question that is in my mind, and I am quite sure that if the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) had been in the house he would have asked it long ago. Where is the money coming from? I am going to ask the Conservatives and the C.C.F. where they would get the money for public spending. Would they raise it by taxation, would they borrow from the banks or would they use the Social Credit system and monetize the wealth of the project itself?
In my estimation these are the only three ways in which such things can be financed, and I should have liked to have heard some of the previous speakers outline their policies for financing the projects which they are advocating. These are important questions and the people of Canada should know the answers, for they would have a terrific bearing on the cost of the project and, in the case of power, on the cost of the power that would necessarily be charged after the project was completed.
We in this group have the answer. We have a cost-free means of financing the development of our power and other resources for the use of our people under a plan of public

Power Development
investment. We hear a lot about the kind of capital that is used in development projects. I am surprised to hear that our C.C.F. and Conservative friends have become so alarmed about United States dollars. I am not so alarmed as long as our governments, and I emphasize this point, are prepared to safeguard our people from exploitation and unfair practices. It can be done and when this is done I think it is not a matter of great importance from what source the money comes.
I do not believe the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) placed United States capital at the head of the list as the desired medium for developing Mica creek. However, there are always those looking for political capital who can twist words around to suit their own train of thought. Speaking for myself and this group and, I believe, for every member in the house may I say that I would certainly like to see our natural resources developed by Canadian capital. We have it stated, I understand, that at the end of the past year there was over $6 billion on deposit in savings accounts of the people of Canada. I often wonder why these people are satisfied to leave that money on deposit, drawing a low rate of interest, and I often ask this question: Why not invest in the future of Canada and the welfare of Canada?
I heard someone here last night in this debate say that Canadians were poor gamblers. That may be so. Perhaps we would rather clip our 3 per cent bonds and be sure than invest in these projects to which there may be attached some risk. But then, if that is our attitude, why do we sit back and blame the Americans if they are prepared to come in, take that gamble and provide the money for the development which we are afraid to tackle?
I am not making any plea for the United States investor. In the development of our Canadian resources I am firmly convinced that the first to enter this field should be the private Canadian citizens. Second, if there is not sufficient capital forthcoming from that source, the required balance should be made up by public investment. In the event that either is not sufficient to provide the development necessary for the welfare of our people, the third and last resort is foreign capital. But I say this. We must have development.
At this point I should like to read a short excerpt from the Revelstoke Review and I would ask the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge)-who is not in the house-to pay particular attention to it. It is dated Invermere. The Windermere section of the Invermere board of trade at their

February meeting heard an address by Dr. Coy, who is the head of their committee, on the Columbia river development.
Dr. Coy pointed out that the Columbia river is the logical source of power for the interior of British Columbia and said that the increase of population and the continued well-being of the people is contingent upon obtaining an adequate and cheap source of energy.
All investigations have shown, he said, that the building of a high dam at Mica Creek is the first step in the development of this river to obtain the necessary hydroelectric energy.
The undertaking can be done, the speaker said, only by agreement between the government of British Columbia, the government of the Dominion of Canada and the government of the United States.
The meeting unanimously passed a resolution presented by Dr. Coy that provincial and federal governments be urged to confer on the problems and place for construction of the dam without further delay and further that the B.C. government, in the opinion of the Windermere district board of trade, would best serve the interests of the people of B.C. by giving sole rights on this project to the B.C. Power Commission.
For the benefit of those in other parts of Canada I may say that the B.C. Power Commission is a public investment corporation in the province of British Columbia for the development of power projects. We are quite proud of that corporation. They have done a splendid job. They have opened up many resources and have provided power in many parts of British Columbia in which I am sure private capital companies would not have provided it.
This whole field of public investment was one of the first things discussed at the beginning of this session. I think we all recall the words of our own Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when he was speaking on federal-provincial relations in the light of the recent conference. It was during the throne speech debate. As reported at page 49 of Hansard, these are his words:
I said we felt that parliament should not provide for sharing in the cost of provincial projects except in special circumstances and as a part of a policy which we could justify on national grounds.
I think those words are well spoken. I think this whole problem of public investment, as I said before, should be entered in order to fill the breach where private capital is unable to fill the bill. As I say, I agree with the- words of the Prime Minister 100 per cent. In fact, I also believe that the less the federal government become involved in provincial affairs, the better for all concerned. But we have a peculiar situation in relation to the development of power on the Columbia river. This government has already declared that such a development is in the national interest. I think all who recall the debate in the house last year will

not dispute that statement. Hence the government-and I mean this national government -is committed to the Columbia development program.
Last year we heard much about the building of the proposed Mica creek dam. We in the interior had high hopes that such construction would be under way this year. But for some reason-and I am not going to lay the entire blame at the door of this government-all plans for the development of the Columbia are at a standstill. We hear nothing about Mica creek. Despite what the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Mac-Eachen) had to say last night-and I hate to question the word of such a learned economist-when he was trying to play down the value of cheap hydroelectric power in industry, we in British Columbia want power. The interior of British Columbia wants it. The province needs it. The whole of Canada would benefit by it. All I can say is this, and I have said it on many other occasions. Let us get down to business and lay concrete plans for immediate action. A few hours around the conference table would clear the way for development and for the opening of a new era in the interior of British Columbia. Most of you will recall the words of Sir Anthony Eden when speaking of the great future in store for Canada. These words were uttered in this house a very short time ago:
I have no doubt that you will fashion it-
He was speaking of the future of Canada.
-in a manner worthy of a great people.
Let us accept that challenge and get on with the job of assuring that great future for our people in British Columbia and in Canada.
