Mr. Speaker, one could not read the words in the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) without some challenge, coming as I do from the province of Saskatchewan. I refer to the words about a joint investment program. We have there, of course, a proposition of which the house has long been aware and one which has been debated often in this house. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I have been in my seat religiously this afternoon expecting to speak following the last Conservative member, namely the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery). A Liberal member and a Social Credit member have come in between us, so I have to make my remarks very short at this time. I realize that the debating time in the evening will be short as it will finish at 8.15.
This project, as I say, is nothing new to this house. It has been the subject of discussion on platforms of all sorts in Saskatchewan,
Power Development
and certainly on political platforms. I do not think there is time here to go into the history of the project, into the origin of it nor the stage which it has now reached. This is the only political comment I shall make when I say it has been held out as political bait in all the federal elections in which I have taken part, and some in which I have not taken part, since away back in 1940. There have been promises, definite promises by Liberal speakers and by the Minister of Agriculture himself. At times we have been assured that those were not actual promises. There is one quotation here which I take from page 1747 of Hansard for February 9, 1953. The minister is quoted by the Regina Leader-Post as having said at a meeting:
The dominion government thus did not need the endorsation of the South Saskatchewan river development association to begin work on the South Saskatchewan river. It has already decided to go through with it ... a decision would he reached on where the dam on the South Saskatchewan should be placed. It would be on one of three sites between the Elbow and Saskatoon. As soon as the site had been finally decided upon contracts would be let, and work would proceed immediately.
Now, there was some dispute later about the accuracy of that report. It was one of those reports which the minister finds so often, in which he had not been correctly quoted. I have dozens. I am not going to talk about what the minister said any more. I am finished with that. I merely want to say that we in Saskatchewan are tired of having this thing trotted out before every election, and then when the election is over, we are blandly told that the time is not ripe; that it is not a national project; that the province is not prepared to assume its proper amount of responsibility, and so forth. So much for the speeches, and so much for the disappointments that we have suffered in the matter.
Now our desire, sir, for this project is, I suppose, born of the depression of the thirties. I think I am quoting the minister here again in a previous debate when he said that during that depression direct relief in Canada amounted to about $186 million. I am going to suggest that the $186 million would go a long way towards building this dam which, to a degree, would take the sting out of any subsequent depression in that part of the country. As the minister knows, and as the Saskatchewan members know, we had a world depression. During that depression eastern Canada suffered, western Canada suffered, as did many other countries.
Not only did the people in the prairie provinces suffer the results of a world depression, but they actually suffered hunger caused by drought. At that time we witnessed settlers

Power Development
shooting their cattle because they could not feed them. I have seen a farmer go down to the station with a buggy and bring back one bale of hay in order to keep alive his last surviving cow from which he obtained milk for his family. When I talk to eastern people and eastern farmers about that particular event I find a lack of realization as to what the suffering actually was. I have seen, as other members have seen, those clouds of dust and those piles of soil accumulate day by day along the telephone poles. We have seen farmers in the southern part of the country loading their family and their small possessions on a hay rack, with perhaps a cow tied behind, heading north to find green grass and water. It just occurs to me here to mention in passing a thing which we have forgotten now, but fundamentally the power of mankind to survive on this earth depends upon the ability of the earth to produce that common and perhaps despised commodity grass.
However, that is enough of philosophy. It is said, and I do not know whether or not it has been proven but I think it has, that the weather is likely to go in cycles. At the moment, as everyone knows, we have an abundance of rain in Saskatchewan. Under the system in which we live, this has produced some of the economic problems from which we are suffering at the moment. But there is this to be said for the type of thing we have now as compared with what we had then: When there is an abundance of food, when there is an abundance of fodder for all the stock, then that type of depression, a depression without money, can be survived on the farm perhaps better than anywhere else.
But if one of these cycles of dry weather should come again, we want to be as well prepared for it as it is possible to be. Of course, that is one of the main reasons why we believe now is the time to build this dam, not at a time when dry weather is upon us. We want this irrigation. We want it for what it has done for Lethbridge. I was struck by what the irrigation project had done in that particular part of the country. I was struck by the diversification of farming there. I was struck by the fact that people now have smaller farms. I was struck by the fact that even if there were dryness in the surrounding area, there was a fodder belt in there that would supply feed for the surrounding starved-out districts. I was struck by the diversification of interests, like sugar beet farming and the substantial industry that has grown there in the fattening of cattle. We would like to have, in our section of Saskatchewan, some of the things that irrigation has

done for Lethbridge and is in the process of doing for Medicine Hat.
Irrigation should bring about an increase in population as a result of the lessening of the size of the acreage held by individuals. Anyone who goes through these plains knows that the scarcity of population is one of the problems that increases our difficulty. We have a tremendous mileage of roads to keep up, even where there are few people. The few children here and there have to be provided with education. Either these little schools have to be kept open or transportation has to be provided for the pupils, as the case may be. The remedy, of course, is population. The population has been dwindling but it is beginning to pick up again. It did dwindle because of the mechanization of the farms, or automation, whatever you like to call it.
Then there is the question of diversification of farming, which I have just mentioned, the feeding of cattle, the growing of sugar beets. There is another thing that one might mention, namely, the attraction of a certain type of immigrant that we might be able to get into our country. I am not going to argue that the failure of immigration, or the comparative failure, this year is a failure on the part of this government, or what is its cause. But there is a fine class of people in northern Europe who would be attracted to an irrigated country, just as in the earlier days many United States citizens were attracted to southern Alberta because they had been accustomed to irrigation on their own farms at home, and were surprised to find they were able to purchase irrigated land at a much lower price than they had paid in the United States.
To my mind, irrigation which would come from a dam of the type desired would-and I have already suggested this-cause an economic stability of which we are not sure at the moment, because our whole economy has been geared to the production of wheat. Even that has failed us this year in that we have been unable to market wheat in the quantities that are satisfactory.
There is also the question of a feed bank. We talk about a bank for wheat, for cereals, for grain, but there is the other question of a feed bank for forage. I do not want to go into that. Some of my agricultural friends and experts in this particular party are much more familiar with it than I am, but I think it is a thing which should be mentioned. I had the unfortunate experience one winter, which I imagine the minister will remember very well, following the summer of 1919, when cattle were dying out there like flies because

they did not have enough to eat. A lot of people got them through the winter, but when they turned them out in the spring onto the dry grass lacking any nourishment, and with the heat of the sun, they simply wilted and that was that. People lost their herds and lost the money they had invested in them.
At the moment, sir, we have a fair start in industrial production in the province of Saskatchewan. It is a fact that is not generally well enough known in other parts of Canada. Certain factories are going to start operations this very year. For example, a pipe factory is to commence operations in the city of Regina. It is to manufacture pipe through which oil or gas may be conveyed. There is an undertaking to produce cement. These things are all tied in with the question of power and irrigation from the project that I have suggested. It is a common economic fact that power of any kind, and particularly cheap power, attracts industry. We have now, of course, a wider distribution of electric power and that process will go on. The distribution and transportation of natural gas, and oil discoveries which are now taking place, are making us at least a rival, if a small one, of our neighbouring province to the west. These things are going on and all of us are beginning to see a great new era for that province which up to a few years ago at least was regarded simply as a great plain where one grew some grain in the summer time and sat close to the stove in the winter time. That was about the only prospect we had. It was with those ideas and in that spirit that a good many settlers came to the province of Saskatchewan.
I am sure a good many of them came there away back at the time the minister came there-I am not suggesting that he or myself was one of those people-with the idea of making as much money as they could and getting away from there as fast as possible. Perhaps in one respect the fact that they were not too well off did us some good because it prevented them from moving out until they had an opportunity to establish worth-while homes, and now they have decided to stay and watch their sons under the new conditions of power, gas and electricity on the farms, and these things that I have mentioned, increasingly better roads, look upon that province as their home and reconcile them to living there with pleasure and with comfort, and with profit, too, may I say. If this government can get the wheat crisis cleaned up as soon as possible, conditions will be even better. Therefore, we need this dam; we need irrigation and we need the power.
Power Development
I said, sir, that I was going to speak briefly, and I did mean that. Some millions of dollars have already been spent on the Saskatchewan river dam in surveying and in engineering, largely through the department under the minister. It is too bad that these moneys should be wasted. The results of their findings are upon the record. Previous to 1949, of course, we were told that the province would not have to spend a cent on this project. In the election promises and in others this was to be purely a federal matter and a federal expenditure, but subsequent to the election of 1949 we came back here to face a minister who smiled at us smugly and said:	Well,
of course, we could go ahead with this program. We have made arrangements. We are going to see what the province will do. I could go into a long story about that. Hansard reports are full of it. I shall refrain from doing that at the moment. In the course of the negotiations that have gone on since that time the province has become pretty heavily committed. I know that in a letter by the premier of the province to the Prime Minister an offer of $72 million was made as the provincial share. At that time the agreed-upon cost, in spite of the Hogg report which preceded it, was to be $135 million in all. Although I have not the figure I believe the province has increased its offer since that time.
In 1954 the minister said there were three main conditions necessary for the starting and the completing of this project. He said that the first one was an interprovincial agreement on the availability of water required for power and irrigation purposes. The first of those conditions was met. The prairie provinces water board agreed that there was plenty of water in the South Saskatchewan and its tributaries to supply water for the project near Outlook.
The second condition was a Saskatchewan commitment toward the cost of the dam. That was the statement at that time. It was to remove any suggestion that Ottawa was subsidizing provincial power production. I have already dealt with that. Letters from the premier of Saskatchewan to the Prime Minister of Canada have continually expressed nothing but co-operation and willingness to be counted in the project so that it could go ahead.
The third stipulation was a realistic estimate of the cost of the project. It is true that we had the Hogg report which was rather unfavourable and which added about $100 million to the cost that I have given, but that report was heavily discounted. It was discounted in this house by the minister himself who said, at least on one occasion, that

Power Development
the cabinet had pretty well written off that particular report. We are then told that the negotiating committee set up by the federal government in conjunction with the provincial government had estimated the costs as follows: main reservoir and dam $80 million; irrigation system $35 million; the power plant $20 million, or a total of $135 million.
Someone might say, well, we have heard it said frequently in the house that the people of Saskatchewan are always complaining about something; they are always wanting something. Well, we are and I do not think that it is a bad thing or an unhealthy thing; but no one has ever suggested in this house or elsewhere that we have not done our share to build up this great country whether in public projects or by any other means. I do not care whether it is by means of war contributions, recruiting of men or payment through taxes to other projects in the country; I do not think anyone can say we have been niggardly in that regard.
When we mention projects like the Canso causeway or the St. Lawrence seaway we do it in commendation of these things. We are glad to see the nation prosper and we believe that through public investment the nation can prosper and that it cannot prosper without it.
I have now concluded what I wanted to say and I now move, seconded by the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Campbell):
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma-

Mr. Speaker, the sub-amendment which has just been moved represents in reality one of the major questions dealt with by the Leader of the Opposition in introducing the motion yesterday on this question which is of such importance to Canada as a whole.
There is no need of saying what the South Saskatchewan dam and irrigation project will mean and what it will achieve in the days that lie ahead when drought returns once more to Saskatchewan. The arguments have been made over and over again and as far as I am concerned it is unnecessary to prove that goodness is good.
The whole proposition is one that has been pushed about by this government for a period

of years. Postponement has followed postponement in relation to its consideration by subterfuge and excuses but until the last two days I doubt whether the people of Saskatchewan will have realized as finally as they now must realize that this necessary project has been written off by this government.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) dealt at some length with this project yesterday as he has dealt with it and supported it on many previous occasions. Indeed, I was rather surprised to hear the hon. member for The Battlefords speak as though he had suddenly made a great discovery that the Conservative party was now supporting this project, a project which this party has supported for many years. Over and over again it has been included in the party platform and over and over again it has received the approbation and firm support of the Leader of the Opposition and the vote of each and every hon. member in this party from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

Having said that, I want to make reference to the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was here yesterday while the Leader of the Opposition was speaking. I realize that the Prime Minister cannot continue to be in the house with all the responsibility that faces him but I do believe that the Prime Minister owed it not only to the people of Saskatchewan but to the people of Canada as a whole to have spoken in this debate and allowed Canadians to learn something of the concept of this government relative to this most important subject contained within the resolution.
As a matter of fact, this has been a campaign of silence on the part of the government in the face of the advancement on the part of the opposition of a policy which is necessary to Canada today and which is not one that advocates the expenditure of money without dividends in the national development.
I think the people as a whole are becoming tax conscious and do not want unnecessary expenditures made. Expenditures for national development are self-liquidating in that they produce a return far above what the actual expenditure amounts to.
. I was rather amazed at the speech of the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart). I think Canadians as a whole, and I have found this to be true as long as I have been a member of this house, do not endeavour to look at problems from a parochial angle. Each citizen endeavours to join together in

a common effort to build all parts of Canada.
I should like to have heard the hon. gentleman advance something in the nature of what the maritimes are asking for, with something of the vision of the maritime members who have spoken during this debate. Instead of that he resorted to a discussion of trivial matters that in no way are of interest to Canadians as a whole.
What of the maritimes? Well, I have visited the maritimes on a number of occasions and have tried to understand something of their problems and something of the need of power development in the maritimes in order to equalize those advantages which central Canada has which are natural to the geographic location of Ontario and Quebec.
I was very much taken by the move a year or so ago for the formation of an Atlantic province economic council and also by the report that was made by Dr. A. G. Christie in which he advocated the pooling of all existing electrical generating systems in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick under a joint power authority, something much in the nature of the plan advocated yesterday on a national basis by the Leader of the Opposition. Under this plan, under this merged system plan, the encouragement of new industries by the providing of reliable electrical and power services at favourable rates would be established. Steam plants would be established in the province of Nova Scotia by reason of the coal that is waiting there for a market, and in the province of New Brunswick there would be hydroelectric developments.
I believe that something in the nature of what is described by this resolution must come about because we are not equally endowed with power potentialities in all parts of Canada. I believe that under this resolution consideration could be given to bringing power to industry. As the Leader of the Opposition has said, today industry goes to power; but I believe that in the new atomic age which we are entering at the present time power will be taken to industry. I am one of those who believe that in certain parts of Canada, the maritimes in particular, atomic energy plants for civilian purposes should be a matter of primary consideration, in addition to the production of power through the medium of coal and hydro sources.
In other words, there should be a national vision to equalize opportunity everywhere in Canada and to enable the building of this nation in the face of the challenge referred to today by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron). The hon. member spoke of the challenge of the U.S.S.R. in the economic
Power Development
world and how socialism provided the answer.
I do not want to get into any argument in that connection, but let me tell my hon. friend that that is the same unrealistic attitude we heard in Saskatchewan. For many years we had theoretical socialism, but when it came to the development of our resources the government of that province, after having entered into various industrial activities quite unsuccessfully, having produced for years but without profit-we got neither-finally decided to invite capital into the province to develop northern Saskatchewan.
When my hon. friend speaks of the challenge of the U.S.S.R. let me say that this industrial challenge is going to be a tremendous one for every part of the free world. The reason is the serf-like wages that are paid, the fact that the agriculturist is required to turn his product over to the state at whatever the state determines, the fact that there is tyrannical control over the hearts of men with each man being a robot under the control of the state. Certainly the U.S.S.R. with its resources and the vast developments which are taking place in connection with power, particularly the establishment of nuclear plants, represent a challenge.
For that reason this resolution more than ever before is of first importance. It is one that affects the people of Canada as a whole. There should be a united people in a great national crusade for the development of Canada to the end that to a greater extent than ever before we in Canada will be developing our own resources here rather than shipping our raw materials to the United States and thereby exporting employment from this country.
I believe in this resolution. It is one that deserves more than the attitude of silence taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and his ministers. It is one that deserves the serious attention of parliament. It has been dealt with throughout in an objective manner, with one exception. I think the ministers owe something more to parliament than to adopt the aggressive silence which this resolution has met. I could say much more, but I know the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Simmons) wants to give a message and for that reason I shall discontinue now.

Mr. Speaker, any discussion on the use and conservation of water across Canada would be incomplete without reference to the water resources of the Canadian northwest, particularly those of the Yukon Territory and northern British Columbia. The natural resources of this northwest area, surrounded on the north and

Power Development
west by Alaska, are minerals, forest cover and water power; they are linked together in the development of the country. In their beneficial development, these resources are all closely associated because low cost power is an essential agency for the economic development of the mining and forest resources.
Not only will electric power from water power sites in our northwest permit the processing of local ores such as those containing silver, lead, zinc, copper, iron, asbestos, etc., but the potential amount of power is so great that it will attract to power sites in the northwest other ores from various parts of the world, including cobalt, bauxite, nickel and titanium.
As most hon. members of this house know, the Northwest Power Industries Limited, a subsidiary of Ventures-Frobisher-Quebec Metallurgical Industries Companies, has been engaged for three years on engineering investigations and surveys of the power potentials of the upper Yukon river waters in the Yukon and northern British Columbia. Information required for the first million horsepower will be pretty well obtained by the end of this year. It discloses that between 4,300,000 horsepower and 4,900,000 horsepower can be developed from the Yukon watershed in power plants that can be built south of Atlin lake.
Power from these plants can be transmitted without difficulty some 45 miles to industrial sites on the Taku river-and as required 360 miles, without difficulty, to the Canadian port of Alice Arm-and to other industrial sites throughout the northwest.
All the investigations and plans have strictly conformed with the Canadian government policy as announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) from time to time in this house, that water power from Canadian waters must be developed in Canada and is to be used in Canada to the fullest extent possible.
In addition to the Yukon river project there are other power resources in the northwest in the watersheds of such rivers as the Liard, Stikine, Dease and the Nass river. All these permit major development.
In fact preliminary investigations reveal that this particular area might afford 6 million horsepower and the Nass river area another half million. This is in addition to the upper Yukon river watershed.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
IMr. Simmons.]

Mr. Speaker, in continuing my remarks, which were interrupted at six o'clock, I should like to say further that there are the power potentials of the Peace river near Finlay Forks and of the Stuart and Babine rivers, these latter being in the vast drainage system of the large lakes of central British Columbia comprising Stuart lake, Trembleur lake, Takla lake and Babine lake. I think it can be stated that the water power resources of our Canadian northwest are greater than the most optimistic estimates made so far. There is every reason to believe that the value of water power and its place in the development of Canada's natural resources will greatly increase over the next 20 years. I am sure that this is one of the things that will be mentioned in the Gordon royal commission report.
The value of waterpower to Canada in dollars and cents will not only be evident in connection with our own resources but the availability of large blocks of power will bring to Canada for processing raw products from all over the world. What an assured future Canada has if she realizes the potential treasures she has in her vast water resources. You can readily see that the northwest has the largest water potential on this continent, so far as I know.
If our resources in the north are to be developed then our resources must be looked upon with more vigour than has been the case heretofore. Canada should, therefore, adopt a policy with regard to the northwest and the rest of Canada's northland which will engender a gradual shift of transportation, population and industrial growth to the northward. Only when this has been recognized and achieved will an adequate development of our resources be realized. If serious consideration is not given to this proposed project it is quite conceivable the result will be that the development of our hydroelectric potential and consequent economic expansion of the whole area through the development of its resources will be retarded for years, if not for generations.
It does not take too active an imagination to appreciate the contribution to the permanent economy of the northwest that a project such as that envisioned by the Frobisher group would make. Neither does one have to indulge in extravagant dreams to visualize what great economic developments would redound to Canada's northwest from future development of this region's natural resources. We need new vision and understanding of what the northwest can mean to our future

as Canadians and to the future of free mankind. We want policies to roll back the frontiers of this country and give Canada depth as well as breadth.
I am informed by Northwest Power Industries Limited that their field work will continue in 1956 to complete the detail surveys necessary for the objective I have outlined in anticipation of commencing actual construction of the first stage of the project in the Taku river area in the not too distant future. Field work planned will include checking of triangulation work, soundings of the Yukon river through Miles canyon and further surveys on the Nakonake river. A large expenditure will be made on diamond drilling on the Miles canyon dam site, at the tunnel entrances, and on the Nakonake river power house site. Sample of borings made will be obtained and studied. It is expected that by the fall of this year the survey period of the Yukon river power project that is necessary to begin construction will be completed.
It is my understanding that a preliminary study by Northwest Power Industries has revealed the Nass river as the most promising interim power area, and surveys will also be undertaken there this coming season. Its power potential is limited but it will be possible to transmit power as required from the Yukon project to the Nass river area. The Nass river project will not in any way prejudice the Yukon project but is insurance that Canada will not lose prospective power customers if there is delay in Yukon power being made available.
There is an important essential in the ordinary development of our water power and that is the rapid obtaining of hydrometric data. The flow of northern streams must be recorded accurately and over as long periods as possible. This means that water readings sufficient for safely estimating power potentials should be under way in adequate scope over all our important streams in the northwest that give promise of water power development. There is no use waiting until interest develops in any particular watershed because it is then too late for any long-term records. This is where I think Canada has been backward and there has been a tendency to wait for a demand for vital information while this should have been available and have been collected over the years.
No one fully familiar with the requirements of power development will question this viewpoint. Personally, I doubt if there are more than two major streams in the northwest out of seven or eight where there is sufficient hydrometric data for a private company or a government owned company to
Power Development
actually determine the amount of firm power available in any watershed. The excellent work being done by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources in the hydrometric field is acknowledged but the data is greatly restricted by insufficient money being voted in this house. I would say that the small amount of funds available for hydrometric work across Canada in the coming year will probably be about one-third of what it should be.
We should have a balanced inventory of our national resources with respect to what we have in the way of minerals and forest products, base metals and chemical resources and construction material, and we should also have comparable information as to where necessary water power or power from thermal units can be obtained. In conclusion I should like to say that I believe the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, which is responsible for the administration of the territories, has vision in carrying out its responsibilities in the development of the northern territories, and I know that the present administration has this forward vision and realizes how important it is for Canada that these northern areas should be developed.
The Frobisher plan will develop the vast known resources of the Yukon territory and northern British Columbia for the benefit of the Dominion of Canada as a whole. Consider the development of timber resources, with ample power to operate pulp and paper mills and the development of mineral deposits in the northwest and from places around the world by the utilization of lost-cost power for smelting and processing ores. Yes, Mr. Speaker, we have a wonderful future in Canada and the northwest.

Mr. Speaker, the grievance I rise to state is the closed mind and the stubborn attitude of my otherwise genial friend, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), in relation to the question of pensions of retired civil servants.
The reasons I raise this matter at this time are several. I need not remind hon. members that I have been concerned about the question for a long time. In addition, certain answers have been given to me recently by the Minister of Finance which would suggest that no consideration is being given to this

Superannuated Civil Servants' Pensions House of Commons. This is during the question period too, Mr. Speaker, and this is what I find under question No. 69:
Major Mott-Radclyffe asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer when legislation to amend the Pensions (Increase) Act will be introduced.

speechtext:
No, it was not. It was as much a surprise to that member as it would be if it took place here. I have been making some reference to what happened in the United Kingdom and I should like hon. members to note this, that the basic principle of providing increases for civil servants because of the increase in the cost of living was established by the wartime coalition government in 1944. I have been particularly interested in the length of time that was spent by the British House of Commons debating the government's bill on that occasion. In this house we all know, because we are reminded of it many times, that debates are handled much more expeditiously in the United Kingdom parliament than they are here. We have been told repeatedly how debates on the address can be handled in a day and a half and so on. I ask hon. members to note this, that in 1944-and members will recall the seriousness of the war situation at that time-the debate on the government's bill to increase pensions occupied 210 columns in the British Hansard over several different days. I give that figure because, as hon. members know, the British Hansard is numbered by columns rather than by pages as is ours. But there are two columns to a page and 210 columns works out to 105 pages.
That is a mark of the seriousness with which members of the parliament of the United Kingdom faced this problem right in the midst of the difficult days of the war in 1944. They occupied 105 pages dealing with the question of increasing the pensions of retired civil servants. Why did they take so long? Because, despite the improvements that the government of the day was proposing in the pensions of retired civil servants, the members were not satisfied. Members of all parties felt that something better should be done and a good deal of the argument turned on such things as means test provisions and other restrictions that were still being imposed on retired civil servants and other pensioners of the United Kingdom.
I feel that not only should I give the house the type of statistics I have listed indicating

the time and attention given to this question in the United Kingdom but I should also like to quote one or two excerpts from speeches made when the 1944 pensions increase bill was introduced. It was, of course, introduced by Sir John Anderson who was then chancellor of the exchequer. In column 1761 of the British Hansard for March 3, 1944, he said this:
The measure which I have to submit to the house carries out a promise made by me on 3rd December last, in the course of the debate on the address.
The amendment which was then under discussion proposed that state and local government pensions should be increased to a level corresponding with the increased cost of living. I said, in the course of the statement which I made on that occasion, that, in the view of the government, the arguments for and against doing something were still fairly evenly and nicely balanced, but, on the whole, the government considered that there was a case for some action. I made it perfectly clear that the government would concentrate attention on cases of what I described as "real, grave hardship".
The chancellor at that point went on to quote from something which he had said earlier but he proceeded to make it clear that, although there were arguments pro and con, particularly in time of war, nevertheless the government accepted the fact that it had a moral obligation to be concerned about the position of those who were suffering real and grave hardship because of the smallness of their pensions. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that everything that was said about real and grave hardships on the part of pensioners in that country and everything that would apply to the situation over there now applies with equal force here, if not more so. I submit that the people to whom I have referred in my statistics as to the numbers who are drawing these small pensions are people who are suffering real and grave hardship and that the government owes to them serious consideration of their position.
I should like hon. members to listen to another few sentences which were spoken during the course of this debate. This time I am free to admit that I am quoting a labour member of the House of Commons but he was a member who was supporting the coalition government of the day and he was actually speaking against some of those independent souls around the house who were trying to persuade the government to do better than was proposed in the house. The labour member whom I am quoting is Mr. Pethick-Lawrence, and he had this to say. It is to be found at column 1777 of the United Kingdom Hansard of March 3, 1944:

-but the fact is that underlying all contracts for payment at some future date there is an assumption, unwritten and unspecified, but nevertheless implied. That is the stability of the purchasing power of money. Unless this is substantially maintained all time-contracts are meaningless.
I commend the entire column or two from which I am now quoting to the Minister of Finance, the Secretary of State and all others who have to deal with this matter, for Mr. Pethick-Lawrence goes very fully into this whole question of pensions being based on contracts and lays it out, in my view, very well that one cannot contend that a contract has been kept if the cost of living has been permitted to rise. Further down he says this. I am still quoting Mr. Pethick-Lawrence:
There is this further point when we are dealing with employees of the state. A private employer may argue that he had nothing to do with fixing the value of money, that it is an act of God so far as he is concerned, God being the state or possibly the Chancellor of the Exchequer.
It is too bad that he does not say "the Minister of Finance" so that it would come a little bit closer to home but I am sure the connection is not overlooked. I continue the quotation:
When the state makes a contract, however, it itself has the power of altering the value of money, and, therefore, the state cannot quite get away with that excuse. Therefore, I have come to the conclusion and I think it is the same conclusion to which the Chancellor has come, although he may not have put it quite so bluntly, that in equity the state must review its contracts to meet the situation.
Mr. Speaker, that is exactly what I asked Mr. Ilsley to do many years ago. That is exactly what I asked Mr. Abbott to do every year that he was minister of finance. That is what I am still asking the present Minister of Finance to do, namely to review these contracts, to recognize the principle of equity 67509-90J
and to do something to meet the situation of our retired civil servants.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that there are those who think that this is just that same old speech being made over again but even Your Honour will admit it is a different speech although it is on the same subject. I know there are those who say, "We are going to have to listen to these speeches as long as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is here." There is one way in which the government can put a stop to the making of these speeches on behalf of the retired civil servants and that is by doing justice to them and bringing in a measure or putting in the estimates at this session an item that will provide for an increase in the pensions of these people and put them on a basis whereby they can cope with today's cost of living.
Let us not hear any more the argument that the government must concern itself with what other employers are doing. I know that the government sometimes takes the view that it must not be the best employer in the country. It should not be the worst either. But I am not satisfied even with the idea that the government should be an intermediate kind of employer. In my view the government as an employer should lead the country, should be a model employer and in this matter should give a lead to other employers and other jurisdictions. Let it not be argued that the old age security pension without a means test takes the place of an increase in these pensions. Other people obtained the old age pension without a means test in addition to whatever other income they had or whatever income they may earn. That is no answer at all to this problem. As a matter of fact, so far as the old age pension is concerned, the Minister of Finance knows what I think should be done about it. I believe the amount of that pension should be increased as well. We shall deal with that matter on another occasion. For the moment we are dealing with this specific problem, namely the plight of our retired civil servants. As strongly as I can I put it to the minister that he should not let another session go by just sloughing the matter off by making the same old answer. This session apparently-and I hope it is true-there is going to be an increase in civil servants' salaries. That is fine. One of the reasons for it is the greater productivity of the country. Another reason is the increased cost of living. Those same reasons make possible and make necessary an increase in the pensions of retired civil servants. I call upon the minister and the government to give the lie to my opening words, when I said that the minister has a closed mind or is stubborn.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take much time, and I may say that I am speaking entirely extemporaneously.
I am wondering why the hon. member who introduced this subject confined his remarks particularly to the civil servants. I do not think he intended to necessarily. I think we can say that the financial policy of the government over the years has been of such a nature that people now retiring with pensions that were at the time of contributing equal in purchasing power to what they expected would give them a fair living, have depreciated considerably so that today the dollar value of the pension has seriously diminished. Now, that of course applies to all pensions, civil service or otherwise.
I know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) perhaps is directly responsible for the civil servants of Canada but because of financial policies that have been pursued the minister is responsible to the entire population of Canada and, in respect to the matter under discussion, all people who may be living on pensions resulting from contributory schemes. I have met retired bank managers, particularly in the cities of Victoria and Vancouver, who had been paying into pension schemes inaugurated by the chartered banks years ago which were looked upon as being fairly healthy pension schemes. What has happened? Those men, honoured in their profession, are now having to live on a pittance. Why is that so? It is not because they do not draw the amount of pension that is due to them, but because

of the depreciation in the value of the dollar in terms of purchasing power.
Now, not only does that apply to bankers but it applies to any class of person who has been on a contributory pension scheme. In a previous session of parliament I once illustrated the point. I visualized a person going to the bank years ago and saving his dollars expecting in the years to come to be able to draw, out money which would be worth so much in purchasing power. I visualized this person in his old age going to the bank and drawing from his savings account perhaps all that he had there. On his way out of the bank he is held up by a robber. In the process a little scuffle takes place and the thug gets away with half the man's savings. Supposing that happened today in reality? What would you discover? You would find that the police would be on the track of the thug, attempting to run him down. If he were caught he would be hailed into court and sent to prison.
Well now, what is the difference? Today the same person who put his savings into the bank many years ago goes to the bank and draws out his savings. He finds that in terms of purchasing power his savings are worth only half what they were worth many years ago. What is the difference? The difference is only this, that the robber who held up the man at the bank was a crook and was sentenced to jail. In the case of the depreciation of purchasing power, it is a matter of the government pursuing a wrong policy that actually robbed the man of half his savings. Now, of course, I am not going to accuse the Minister of Finance or the government of being dishonest men. I would say that they are pursuing financial policies which, in themselves, are not honest. Until they can arrive at a policy whereby the purchasing power of our money is retained over the years, then we will always have this very aggravated situation of the depreciation of the value of one's savings, whether it is in the bank or whether it is put into a pension fund. The financial policy being pursued by the government now, in reality, is a steal-not that they have stolen money personally, not that they have been, in themselves, dishonest, because I think they are honourable men trying to pursue what they regard as honourable policies. But in reality the policies are dishonest by reason of the fact they filch from the people their purchasing power.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I need say no more. I do not believe the problem can be remedied merely by the Minister of Finance saying, "Well, we will increase the pensions because the cost of living has increased and of course we will tax the rest of the country

to pay the pensions." Now, that might be all right as a temporary thing but it does not get to the heart of the trouble. It does not get to the disease that is eating away the body. We must correct the financial policy of the country in order to stabilize our dollar so that its value does not fluctuate as it has over the years in terms of purchasing power. I do not believe there will be a solution found until a right financial policy is pursued that will get to the heart of the trouble.

speechtext:
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) has more or less confused the issue by bringing in the question of inflation and the depreciation of the dollar. If any monetary philosophy calculated to depreciate the value of the dollar was ever conceived before, it is certainly the philosophy of social credit. These people would have money printed in a way that would, in the words of Social Credit members, equate the money supply with production. It is that very thing that has caused the depreciation of the dollar in Canada. There is more money in circulation in relation to the amount of production than there was some 30 or 40 years ago or even 10 years ago. This, in itself, has caused the pensioner to be in an adverse position today.
I am not one who wishes on every occasion to support the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I would think there would be more sincerity in his undertaking if he did not rise on almost every occasion to find some way of reducing the power of the government to raise money. Only recently the hon. member introduced a motion calling for certain reductions in the tax revenue by removing the 3 per cent floor on medical expenses. I am sure that either he has, or some members of his party have, already indicated that the income tax exemptions should be raised. That again would mean a loss to the federal treasury. Someone near me in this section of the house has calculated the additional money that would be required if we had undertaken all of the measures proposed by the C.C.F. party during this session. It runs into something over $1,500 million. The hon. member himself will not feel that I am being unfair when I say that I doubt somewhat the sincerity of his proposals.
The question that the hon. member raises at this time affects almost everyone on a fixed pension. Pensions that are based on contributions made ten, fifteen, twenty, or even thirty years ago are totally inadequate today and no one denies that fact. There is something entirely wrong with our pension
Superannuated Civil Servants' Pensions system that is based on contributions made in an economy such as ours where there is no absolute control such as the socialists would wish to have. It seems to me that if we were to follow the philosophy of the Social Credit party it would also mean almost absolute control of prices, wages and so forth. So long as we allow prices to fluctuate-and they do-pensions will not be satisfactory. When 1 say "fluctuate" it probably does not adequately describe what does take place in our economy because if we go back to 1900 we shall find that wages averaged around $2 a day. Even up to 1925 they were around $3 or $4 a day. When contributions are made on that basis the pensions cannot possibly be adequate. Wages are now running at $2 an hour, $15 and $16 a day, and in many instances up to $18 and $20 a day. Therefore, one can see the inadequacy of pensions provided both by the civil service and by industry on that basis. Pensions should be based on the cost of living at the retirement age. I know of many industries employing large groups that do favour that type of pension plan. The pensions paid are paid on a basis of length of service and on the highest last ten years' earnings or the last five years' earnings, whichever is the greater. That is a reality that should be faced. I am sure it is more important actually than paying $40 a month which hon. members across the way were so insistent was the requirement, $40 a month to people who might be earning $5,000, $10,000 or $15,000 a year. They said that $40 a month must be paid to every one of those independent people. It does appear in our budget and creates the impression that a very large sum of money is being paid out. In reality it is returned even before it is paid out, but it does appear as a budgetary expense. For that reason it is very difficult to make an increase based on some millions of pensions.
Let me get back to the people who are living on a very low income; that is, on a pension based on earnings made some thirty or forty years ago. Certainly, it is very difficult to imagine how they sustain themselves. I am fairly well acquainted with two large companies that within the last few months have increased pensions to those who were retired prior to the rapid increase in wages and prices that has taken place since 1950. They have increased their pensions from a low figure of $1 to $50 a month, depending on the length of service of the pensioners and their earnings at that time. Perhaps we should face this question. But when facing it, it would be more appropriate for the members of the opposition to face the realities of the situation, namely, how are we to raise the money for

Superannuated Civil Servants' Pensions that purpose, and not on every occasion be faced with want of confidence motions which supporters of the government have to vote against. I refer to those very popular motions asking for a reduction in taxes here and there. Let us have a little more sincerity over this problem. Let us all face the facts truthfully and I am sure we shall be able to do better for everyone.

I speak with some considerable knowledge of the conditions in which many of these people are living today, because many of them live in the constituency that I represent. That is not surprising, since it is of course the most salubrious part of Canada. I hear mutterings from around me about that. Of course, it is an incontestable fact, otherwise retired civil servants would not come there in such large numbers. Nevertheless I do think, sir, that as the responsible body in Canada for the conduct of our affairs we in this house should very seriously consider the position in which many faithful servants of the Canadian people are left in their latter years. In my constituency I am continually coming across men and women up in years who are now forced to scrape and scrimp and just get by after years of service in the public service at what I think we will all agree are not particularly generous or extravagant salaries.
In fact, I think it is not too much to say that the salary rates of civil servants are to some extent based on the assumption of security of tenure and an adequate pension at retirement age. Owing to the reasons that many hon. members have stressed here tonight those pensions are now totally inadequate.
I remember some years ago in the provincial legislature of British Columbia we faced the same problem with regard to civil servants and to teachers who are not, of course, civil servants strictly speaking. It was decided at that time that, in spite of the actuarial arguments against increasing the pensions, some action had to be taken because many of these people were in desperate straits. At that time the provincial legislature did place in the superannuation funds governing the pensions of these people a large sum of money to increase pensions for those who had been pensioned some years before. In spite of the discouraging shake of the head just now I would urge the minister to consider seriously the plight of these people who have served so well and faithfully for many years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am assuming that all those who wish to speak on the particular matter that is under discussion have spoken.
I should like to mention briefly another matter before the house votes on the question as to whether you can leave the chair. My grievance arises out of a subject matter that was discussed actively in the industrial relations committee last session while the Unemployment Insurance Act was under review. I am quite sure that if the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) were in his seat at the moment he would recall this particular discussion quite well.
The subject matter of my grievance arises out of the fact that, in spite of that discussion

and in spite of the assurance that was given to us in committee by the Minister of Labour at that time, employees of hospitals throughout this country are still not able to secure the benefits of unemployment insurance in like manner with others in similar positions employed by other employers.
My understanding is that at the present time the only regulation which brings hospital employees under the coverage of the act is one affecting only casual employees. I have a letter which I received recently from the secretary of the hospital employees union in British Columbia which indicates to me that the non-medical employees of hospitals in British Columbia are covered only in the case of two hospitals where they have succeeded in negotiating with their employers and by consent they have been brought in under coverage of the hospital insurance act.
Last year when the Unemployment Insurance Act was under review I argued quite vigorously but unsuccessfully against the inclusion in the new act of a principle which as far as I can recall affects only hospital employees, employees of charitable institutions with the exception also of employees of the crown in right of the province, and that principle is that they can be brought under coverage only with the consent of the employer.
I objected most strenuously, as I say, to the continuance of that principle within the act and suggested that if the phrase had been changed to read, "on application of the employees," it would have been a much more equitable arrangement and would have been one which would have allowed employees in perhaps certain types of hospitals who did not wish to come in to remain outside the coverage of the act. Nevertheless the act was passed in that form but in the committee the Minister of Labour did state, as recorded on page 255 of the minutes of the committee, that the matter was under active consideration by the cabinet after having received the recommendation of the unemployment insurance commission and the unemployment insurance advisory commission.
This was a recommendation which would have brought in the entire list of employees which the Minister of Labour set forth as recorded on page 253 of the proceedings. This list of employees included:	clerks, stenographers, secretaries, bookkeepers, switchboard operators, laundry workers, stationary engineers, firemen and other power-house workers, carpenters, painters, electricians, plumbers and other building construction workers, porters, elevator operators, chauffeurs, drivers and other transport workers, gardeners and other ground maintenance
Unemployment Insurance-Hospital Workers workers, printers, machine operators and other craftsmen, and all categories of employees who normally come under the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act when employed by other employers.
In spite of what I felt to be the almost certain assurance when the committee rose last year, that long before this these employees would by regulation of the commission have been brought in under the coverage of the act, this has not been done. I rise at this time to express as a grievance the fact that as far as my knowledge goes such employees are still excluded from the benefits of the act.
